title: Have You Been to the Sixth-Worst McDonald’s in America?
author: Brendan Fitzgerald
content:
There is virtually no way I could have resisted Sylvie McNamara’s dispatch from her journey to a disreputable McDonald’s in Stafford, Virginia. I’ve listened to my share of the Doughboys podcast, and regularly debate burger rankings with my son. What’s more, I went to high school just two miles down the road from this particular location, whose aggregated Google reviews won it dubious distinction in a nation of interchangeable fast-food franchises. Thankfully, McNamara’s lighthearted investigation, which invites readers to consider Robert Caro and teenage commitments to the social contract, will satisfy you no matter your relationship with the Golden Arches. It reminded me of tongue-in-cheek alt-weekly features, a few pleasurable Paris Review web essays, and that episode of Mystery Show where Starlee Kine goes deep with a Ticketmaster employee. Ba-da-ba-ba-ba, I loved it.

I asked the employee for an explanation. “I think I can give you real insight,” he said. “It be the certain workers we got.” He himself is a high schooler, but he said that “we’re starting to get more younger managers. As soon as they turn 18, they’re getting a manager spot. I think my general manager’s 20. It’s a lot of kids getting these manager titles and positions, but they’re not really managers.”

I told him that to be honest, that environment sounded kind of fun.

Tasty features about fast food in America

Can Jollibee Beat American Fast Food at Its Own Game?

Yasmin Tayag | The Atlantic | December 9, 2025 | 2,832 words

“The U.S. introduced fast food to the Philippines. Now Jollibee is serving it back to America.”

How America Got Its Baby Back, Baby Back, Baby Back

Dan Kois | Slate | August 11, 2025 | 4,865 words

“Chili’s was once a relic of the ’90s. Then it blew past its competitors—and conquered casual American dining. In its Texas test kitchen, I saw how.”

The Tale of the Early-Round KO of Muhammad Ali’s Champburger

Dan McQuade | Defector | February 28, 2025 | 3,775 words

“Ali may have continued to get his free burgers, but he never did get those hundreds of locations.”

author: @NewYorker
content:

title: The Man Who Taught Us How to Pay Attention
author: Brendan Fitzgerald
content:
John Berger spent a meaningful portion of his life thinking, with precision and care, about how to look at the world—an effort he detailed in numerous essays and books, among them Ways of Seeing and About Looking. “Reading them, you often feel you’re standing next to him in the museum or even looking through his eyes at a painting or a sculpture,” writes A.O. Scott. “You pay attention to his attention.” Scott, an attentive reader himself, brings Berger’s lifelong project into our famously distractable era; his consideration of Berger is a primer for observation and study, a gentle nudge to focus, lest we lose sight of something essential.

Right now, we’re in the midst of an attention crisis, individually and collectively snared in an infinite scroll of disruption and distraction. Berger saw this crisis coming and foresaw its consequences. In 1978, writing about photography and its impact on the modern world, he argued that the dominance of images “creates an eternal present of immediate expectation: Memory ceases to be necessary or desirable. With the loss of memory, the continuities of meaning and judgment are also lost to us.” That diagnosis seems even truer today, as the functions of remembering, judging and interpreting are increasingly offloaded from human minds and communities into the ether of social media feeds and artificial intelligence. We’re in danger of forgetting how to look.

More essays on looking deeper

A.O. Scott’s Poetry Lessons

Jonathan Farmer, A.O. Scott | Slate | April 13, 2025 | 2,408 words

“A conversation with the NYT critic on his popular close reads of poems.”

Up a Creek

David Schurman Wallace | The Baffler | October 7, 2026 | 5,890 words

“Nature writing after everyone stopped paying attention.”

The Only Home He Ever Knew

Wendell Brock, Paul Kwilecki | The Bitter Southerner | June 26, 2024 | 6,957 words

“Today, photo geeks the world over consider Paul Kwilecki a master of the documentary form.”

title: A Global Anti-Right Backlash
author: @NewYorker
content:
On a hazy Monday morning in Chandigarh, a city in northern India, Anish Gawande woke up early to check the news he had fallen asleep waiting for. Some nine thousand miles and eight time zones away, Brazil’s President, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, had emerged the winner of his country’s Presidential runoff, a victory that two weeks earlier had seemed improbable. But the left-wing incumbent defied the polls and the prediction markets, mounted a campaign that turned tens of thousands out into the streets, mobilized countless more through social-media apps, and pulled in millions of voters who had not cast their ballot for him in the first round, earlier in the month. Lula’s comeback was inspiring to Gawande, a national spokesperson of one of India’s opposition parties and a voluble critic, on the evening news shows and social media, of the right-wing Hindu-nationalist government of Prime Minister Narendra Modi. In 2020, Gawande had protested the Modi government’s hosting of Brazil’s then President, Jair Bolsonaro—the convicted coup-plotting father of Flávio Bolsonaro, the far-right challenger whom Lula defeated Sunday—as India’s chief guest for its annual Republic Day commemorations. Bolsonaro’s documented homophobia and his acceleration of the deforestation of the Amazon rain forest seemed, to Gawande, an echo of the divisive, destructive politics of Modi’s Bharatiya Janata Party.

In recent months, Gawande has supported and defended the Gen Z uprising that has rocked Modi’s rule, with authorities unable to stamp out rolling protests in New Delhi and other Indian cities. The mass demonstrations, Gawande told me, have “revived the space for dissent in the country,” amid widespread anger over both an economy that has failed to create enough jobs for India’s huge population of young people and an increasingly autocratic politics where more than a hundred and thirty million people have been knocked off voter rolls on dubious grounds. Gawande saw a lesson in Lula’s ability to rally a diverse coalition of movements and parties in the perceived defense of Brazilian democracy. “What Lula’s victory demonstrates is that perhaps it is possible to craft solidarities between these movements, to assemble a rainbow coalition that can take on the might of Modi’s B.J.P.,” Gawande told me. He posted on Instagram, “If it happened in Brazil, it can happen in India.”

In this optimism, Gawande was joined by politicians far afield. After years of gloom in the shadow of President Donald Trump, Modi, Bolsonaro, and others of their ilk, progressives and liberals around the world are finding cause to celebrate. The center-left Spanish Prime Minister, Pedro Sánchez, who has called a snap election in the coming weeks against an emboldened right, declared, “What has happened in Brazil will happen in Spain,” adding, “The comeback of global progressivism has just begun.” Dominique de Villepin, a former French Prime Minister, said that Lula’s victory is “a major signal of hope,” even for France, where the far right is favored to win power in the Presidential elections next year, and where mass protests continue around the country. “The democrats have won the first round of a grand global referendum on democracy,” he wrote on X about Lula’s win.

Like the triumphalism of many from the West’s far right in earlier election cycles, such enthusiasm may be short-lived, a moment of transcendence soon to be subsumed by the churn of polarization and the sclerosis of daily politics. Sánchez’s plans on keeping his job hinge on, at best, cobbling together enough votes to form a stronger coalition than the minority government he currently leads. In India, the B.J.P. retains outsized control over the apparatus of state, the media, and the courts. In Brazil, inflation is high and public debt is surging, and the legislature and state governments are dominated by Lula’s opponents. But his win has blocked what seemed an inexorable advance of the right across Latin America, where left-leaning governments have fallen in rapid succession over the past two years, and has thwarted the Bolsonaros’ broader project of judicial overhaul at home and the potential yoking of Brazil’s foreign policy to Trump’s hemispheric agenda. Ahead of the runoff, Lula cast himself as the defender of Brazilian sovereignty from the predations of Washington and U.S. tech giants, and as the ally of working people against callous élites—he didn’t shy away from his own brand of populism. In the election’s aftermath, Bolsonaro briefly attempted to claim that the result was illegitimate, but he saw right-wing heads of state in South America recognize Lula’s victory. On Wednesday, Bolsonaro, who is under investigation for corruption, money laundering, and tax evasion, for accepting millions of dollars from a disgraced financier to produce a movie about his father, landed in Miami after fleeing Brazil. (Bolsonaro has not been formally charged and has denied any wrongdoing.)

Between the defeat of Bolsonaro this past week and events earlier this year in Hungary, where the long-ruling nationalist Prime Minister Viktor Orbán was ousted in elections, the White House has lost two hugely symbolic allies in its broader right-wing global culture war. By Wednesday, no clear winner had emerged in the Israeli election, in which Trump had endorsed Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, and which saw a historic turnout of Arab voters. And the U.S. President may be humbled further in next week’s midterms, as Democrats eye taking both the House and the Senate. Former President Barack Obama, while stumping for Democrats in Ohio, blasted the Republicans in terms that would have been familiar in Brazil and elsewhere, pointing to the wealthy élites and tech titans who “are able to buy and sell elections like never before,” in service of a Republican Party that “now seems to stand for corrupt government, or inept government, or no government.”

Lula withstood an anti-incumbency challenge on the same day that another once indomitable leader succumbed to one. The Serbian President, Aleksandar Vučić, a close Orbán ally, an erstwhile friend of the Kremlin, and a right-wing strongman effectively in power since 2012, saw his bid to stay in office by running to be Prime Minister foiled by an upstart student movement. The slate of candidates from its de-facto party, called the Student List, outperformed Vučić’s Serbian Progressive Party, and he conceded. The students had been protesting since 2024, when the deadly collapse of a canopy outside a train station in the city of Novi Sad triggered a revolt over perceived state corruption and mismanagement. The protests, which were met at times with sweeping police repression, were resilient, and morphed into a strategic political project that persevered in the face of Vučić’s tactics, which included using state-media channels to tar the students as foreign stooges abetting a deep-state globalist agenda. Now they are trying to figure out how to form the next government in Belgrade, and, like Orbán’s opponents in Hungary, they have embarked on a campaign to reinforce the rule of law in the country and to purge state institutions of those who enabled their autocratic capture.

Those efforts are being mirrored elsewhere. “The vision of Serbian youth converges with that of many other young Europeans,” Nathalie Tocci, an Italian political scientist and former foreign-policy adviser to top E.U. officials, wrote in La Stampa. She pointed to the series of protests convulsing the Continent: there’s the Flamingo movement in Albania—where demonstrations have pulled in a cross-section of society, including students and professionals, infuriated by the government’s handling of a project backed by Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner to open a luxury resort along a coastal ecological preserve, and have surfaced wider public rage against oligarchs in the country. And then there are those who have marched in recent weeks in France, Belgium, Spain, and Italy, calling for access to affordable housing, relief with the cost of living, and greater investment in their schools. “It is a vision of democracy, equality, and social, environmental, international, and intergenerational justice,” Tocci added. “A vision and a commitment expressed through street protests.”

Of course, that’s not the universal view of the unrest. In the chaotic recent scenes from Paris and other French cities, in particular, members of the American and European right have sought confirmation for their culture-war talking points, laying the blame for the vandalism, fires on the boulevards, and looting on Muslim migrants and the alleged leftist extremists who appease them. Online, some Republicans and their supporters linked the chaos to the supposedly globalist world view of Democrats, invoking the spectral menace of communists and jihadists storming through the West’s fallen capitals. But that hysteria misses deeper realities, including the entrenched traditions of confrontational protest in France.

Political Islam has nothing to do with these protests. The unrest began with students unhappy about conditions in their schools and universities, but ballooned into something far larger, activating a swathe of French society that reviles the perceived neoliberalism of President Emmanuel Macron and wants to see greater public investment. It also pulled in apolitical opportunists who participated in the looting, while the government blamed the “ultra left.” Like the Gen Z protests in New Delhi earlier this summer, the protests, which were largely peaceful, were met at times with a crushing police response. Yet some observers have warned that the actions of a minority of the crowd—ransacking businesses and an arson attack that gutted the town hall of Limoges—may be strengthening the hand of the far-right leader Marine Le Pen. Macron is profoundly unpopular, complicating the path for a centrist successor next year. The protesters see their revolutionary zeal as offering a kind of renewal to a flagging French republic—one of their slogans is “On refait 1789 pour ne pas revenir en 1939,” that is, “We are redoing 1789 so as not to return to 1939.” Whether a majority of French voters will be persuaded by the spectacle of the barricades remains to be seen.

There’s no simple narrative bringing together all the separate uprisings. “They are dispersed points of resonance that still need to be tuned to one another,” the Belgian philosopher Michel Feher told an interviewer. Sánchez, in Spain, called the snap election when his ruling coalition was unable to pass housing legislation that many Spaniards had been demanding. In India, anger over the administration of school-board exams snowballed into a larger rebellion against Modi’s illiberal, majoritarian rule. But Matthew Cebul, a researcher on nonviolent resistance movements at the Harvard Kennedy School, sees all these protests as rooted in a universal desire for accountability from one’s government and rage at perceived graft and cronyism. “Illiberal governments thrive on this aura of inevitability or perceived social dominance, but illiberalism is ultimately hollow and vulnerable, especially when it performs poorly,” Cebul told me. He added, “People do not like being governed by crooks and thugs. They want competent governance, not arrogant corruption, and democracy movements can and are winning people over when they call for something better.” ♦

title: Vultures Help Eliminate Pathogens. Bird Flu Could Eliminate Them - Nautilus
content:
Vultures might not be the most charismatic birds, but they do perform an important job. As carrion-feeding scavengers, they dispose of decaying animal matter, even bones, right down their throats. As part of this garbage collection duty, they also neutralize pathogens, routinely gobbling up tissue that’s festering with rabies, anthrax, and botulism and disposing of it in their highly acidic stomachs. 

Of course, vultures aren’t entirely invulnerable to infection. With 16 of 23 vulture species already designated as threatened, the H5N1 avian flu could wreak havoc on their dwindling numbers. Now a team of biologists is sounding the alarm about what declining vulture populations could mean for ecosystems (and us) and issuing a call to action in a letter published in Conservation Biology.

Read more: “We’ll Miss the Vulture”

As carrion feeders, vultures are on the frontlines of the H5N1 panzootic (animal pandemic). They’re not just at risk of contracting the virus from their meals, but from the other vultures who gather around carcasses. Sharp upticks in infections could cause precarious populations to collapse. 

“The greater the number of infected carcasses, the greater the risk of contagion for the vultures,” letter author Jon Morant of the University of the Basque Country explained in a statement. “Since these carcasses can become sources of infection, a paradox arises: As more vultures die, the capacity to eliminate the carrion reduces, the pathogens spread and contagion increases.”

But there’s hope for stalling this positive feedback loop, and the authors outlined a series of steps conservationists and wildlife managers can take to fight back. First, vulture populations should be closely monitored for signs of infection, with special attention paid to migratory species that cross international borders, like the Egyptian vulture. Populations that are most threatened should be vaccinated, the team says, noting that there’s already a vaccination program in place for the California condor. 

Next, vulture feeding stations should be well-stocked with uninfected meat and those that work with vulture populations should suit up. “They must comply strictly with biosecurity protocols (use gloves, masks and protective equipment), especially when working with small populations or with threatened species,” Morant said. The team also recommends that these steps and any additional actions are implemented in a context-sensitive manner that takes into account the socioeconomic conditions of the countries where vultures live.

H5N1 isn’t just a threat to birds, it can currently infect cattle, pigs, and domestic pets, and every new host the virus adds to the list becomes one more opportunity to jump into humans. By protecting our frontline carcass-eating defenders, we can also help protect ourselves.

title: Men Who Eat More Plant-Based Protein Have Higher Testosterone Levels - Nautilus
content:
There’s a testosterone crisis in America—at least according to a number of Trump administration officials. Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., for example, has bemoaned the low-T of the American youth, and even boosts his own levels with testosterone replacement therapy. He’s also a major proponent of eating animals, celebrating the prominent position of meat and dairy in the new food pyramid the US Department of Agriculture unveiled at the beginning of this year.

But a study published last month in the International Journal of Food Sciences and Nutrition suggests Kennedy might be able to ease up on the testosterone shots if he ate more vegetables.

A team of nutritional and metabolic scientists analyzed the four-day dietary intake and hormone levels of more than 2,500 middle-aged men living in Finland. It’s worth noting that the data in their study were also middle-aged, collected during the Kuopio Ischaemic Heart Disease Risk Factor Study between 1984 and 1989.

Read more: “The Impossible Strength of the Testosterone Myth”

After dividing the men into four groups according to their protein intake and controlling for other variables, the researchers found that the subjects’ testosterone levels seemed to be linked to the kind of protein they preferred. On average, the men who ate more meat and dairy had slightly lower testosterone levels. In contrast, those who got more of their protein from plant-based sources had slightly higher levels of the sex hormone. The scientists observed a similar dynamic with their levels of sex hormone binding globulin, a protein that controls how much free testosterone is available in the blood stream.

Drilling down into the dietary data, the team discovered dairy was most responsible for the relatively low-T in the animal protein group. The plant protein group’s higher testosterone levels showed a closer association with protein from vegetables, rather than cereals.

The researchers said they aren’t entirely sure why the protein source appears to affect male sex hormone levels, but said the pattern may be mediated by inflammation. Higher levels of C-reactive protein, a molecule involved in inflammatory pathways, have been linked to reduced overall testosterone levels and those who eat more plant protein typically have lower levels of C-reactive protein.

Additionally, while the researchers controlled for a number of health and lifestyle variables, it’s possible that the plant-eating group had healthier habits overall. But because this is a cross-sectional observational study, causation is impossible to pin down.

Of course, there are plenty of other reasons to limit meat intake—both for your own health and the planet’s. In fact, a new international food pyramid released this week recommends getting the bulk of your calories from plants instead of animals. Testosterone-maxxing might just be an attractive bonus.

title: Dear Human, Poetry Might Save Us from the Apocalypse - Nautilus
content:
When we tell the storyof how we survived the collapse, we might say: like birds, we learnedto move as one.We grew lighterand lengthened our wings.

These are the final lines of “Dear Human at the Edge of Time: A Community Poem.” Assembled from the contributions of 14 different writers across the United States, the poem tells a story about the future that is simultaneously devastating and hopeful.

In the three years since the poem was penned, the question of how we might collectively survive collapse has become an increasingly pressing one. It turns out, we are not paying enough attention to the birds. We have not learned to move as one.

The poem was published in 2023 by Poets for Science in connection with the Fifth National Climate Assessment, which revealed that climate change was already ravaging every region of the United States through rising temperatures, punishing drought, savage wildfires, and deadly storms.

READ MORE: Poetry Gives Us Power

But humanity continues to fall short of the change needed to keep the Earth on a safe course for future generations. The data on climate change have told a clear story for a long time, but that story is not getting through.

Could art and poetry dedicated to conservation themes help ignite a greater feeling of urgency about our predicament and map a way forward? Poets for Science, forged in the turmoil of the first Trump administration, has made this call to action one of its missions.

The group is uniting poets and scientists in collaborations that aim to make the science of conservation both felt viscerally and understood intellectually. It’s also inviting the public to participate with verse or other creative work of their own.

The poem “Dear Human” lives on an interactive platform that allows anyone to contribute. Writers can respond to poems published in an award-winning climate poetry anthology, add to a digital gallery of climate art, or build their own “found poems” out of text borrowed from the Fifth National Climate Assessment.

“Why not poetry?” says poet David Hassler, who co-founded Poets for Science together with American nature poet Jane Hirshfield in 2017. In just a couple of weeks, Poets for Science will hold its first in-person gathering, where scientists and poets will meet across three days to explore the connections between their disciplines, and ways to inspire the civic imagination. That meeting is sponsored by the Wick Poetry Center at Kent State University in Ohio, which Hassler directs.

I spoke with Hassler recently about how poetry is like lichen and how it can help make science meaningful while inspiring collective action.There have been many periods across history when art and science were closely aligned. Artists were scientists and scientists were artists. Nobel laureate neuroscientist Eric Kandel beautifully describes such a period in Vienna at the turn of the 20th century in his book The Age of Insight. The Renaissance, too, was packed with figures who merged artistic mastery with scientific inquiry. But during the scientific revolution, art and science split. There was this intellectual divide. Today it seems like the pendulum might be swinging back the other way. What do you make of this shift?

Yes, all these collective efforts have been co-arising all around the globe, people pursuing similar intersections of science and humanities and arts. It’s what we have discovered in pulling together this Poets for Science gathering. You know, we’re not alone. When we started Poetry for Science in 2017, we were tapping into a collective nerve that I think is shared by so many people. And it’s really been growing over the past 10 to 15 years.

In a recent interview, I was reminded that the word “scientist” was coined in the mid 1800s. Before that, they were “natural philosophers.” There’s this divide between our belief that over here’s my rational thinking, and over there’s my emotional thinking. Here’s my scientific inquiry and over there’s my creative expression.

This divide has been exacerbated by our biases and our technology. I think that it has come to a breaking point, where people are hungering to integrate facts with feelings, so that what we’re learning through the facts of science has meaning in our lives, emotionally and in our lived experience. Perhaps this need to be intentional about bringing them back together in conversation has happened out of an awareness of our failure at progress. We’re feeling sicker. We’re feeling more divided, more alone, more unhealthy, and there’s been a kind of quiet desperation.

We’re also looking for creative solutions to intractable problems in our collective lives and AI is making us question what it means to be human. There’s this attack on the humanities, and tech bros are saying we just need to be good bots. Maybe there’s a moment here where we’re infusing the arts back into our rational scientific thinking because we need to remind ourselves what it means to be human and what we value about being human. Scientists are trying to remember that the questions they ask and the work they do is informed by their humanness, by their cultural background, their emotional lives, their beliefs, their lived experience.Do you think that poetry does something for science or for public understanding of science that other art forms can’t?

I think all art forms can help us make meaning and carry grief and hold our sense of awe and to use that as an energy source, to contain it and to give it shape. All art can do that.

But here’s what poetry can do: It can take the natural metaphors of science and highlight them. We’re not inventing them. If I say that we’re having a “mycelial” conversation, you know what I mean, because we now understand how a mycorrhizal network in soil helps trees communicate with each other and share signals of nurture, but also warning, through this fungal network, this mycorrhizal network.

I think that the language we use to describe the world not only influences how we behave toward the world, it truly influences what we’re able to actually see in the world. The root word of science means to know from Latin, and I think the economy of language in a poem helps us carry new knowledge into the world. And that’s gone a long way. We have been told over and over again that poets are now feeling inspired and getting prompts for their writing from scientific articles and using the language of science in their poems.

But it’s working both ways. Scientists are saying they’re turning to poetry. We have so many poems on the poetsforscience.org global gallery and in this anthology The Nature of Our Times written by scientists. Why? They say that they don’t have a place in their scientific paper or essay to put their emotional language. The poems offer a place to put their awe and grief and fear. Many scientists also say they’re using the arts and humanities to help them shape the questions they ask and the directions they go in their scientific inquiry. Laura Valski, for instance, talks about how in her research with ecology [in Washington State], she’s attuned to the stories of the native people of that region and of the language they use to inform the questions she asks.

I love what Jane Hirshfield says, that the metaphor and the microscope are both instruments of discovery.

Yes, metaphor stems from metapheran in Greek, its origin. It means to carry, to cross over. In a sense, we’re carrying new knowledge over from science into our emotional lives through language and metaphor. And that’s how it can bring change.

Obviously, science is many things. Not just conservation, but also technology, so it’s AI and surveillance cameras, or it’s building weapons.

Yes, and some kinds of poetry are used by dictators to influence mass crowds and to hypnotize people. The spell of poetry can be used for good and for bad. So can science. Both of them are that powerful.

How do you grapple with this darker side of science and poetry when you encourage collaborations?

The 14th century poet Rumi said your intention does all the work. We do it with care and with the right intention and with rigor and with honesty. I’m not writing a poem to influence your behavior for my gain. I’m writing a poem because I have an intention to speak a truth that is authentic to me. The paradox is that if I can speak authentically and truthfully about my own idiosyncratic personal life, only then can it have a power that speaks to others and help them find their own meaning from it.

So, yes, we can create nuclear weapons and toxic chemicals. I just watched this frightening documentary about the pesticides that we’re using in agriculture that are destroying our soil, our health, and our bodies. Those chemicals were invented by a German scientist for warfare in World War II. The companies literally took the research that was being done for warfare and tweaked it to use on our crops. How’s that for an image?

In the essay you write that art without science risks inspiring ineffective action. Why is that?

If I don’t understand how mycelial networks actually work and I wanna write a poem about mycelium, then perhaps what I’m writing might work as a poem, but it doesn’t help me understand the forest and act in ways that create the conditions for that forest to thrive. We have a crisis of science communication, which was the origin of the Poets for Science movement in 2017, so poems can help us make meaning and speak to our own lived experience and our emotional lives. And by doing that, to make meaning of science.

This Poets for Science initiative began in response to the actions of the first Trump administration, and out of desperation, anger, grief, and fear. Jane Hirshfield wrote a poem, and that poem went around the world essentially in 2017. And then she called me, and said, “Can you help me?” And I said, “Of course.” And our design team put together 23 seven-foot banners of poems about science that she curated. We went to the National Mall for the very first March for Science on Earth Day. Poets for Science had a teach-in tent. There was never room for anybody to sit because it was constantly full the whole day.

What do successful poems about conservation like Hirshfield’s get right?

I avoid rating this poem over that poem and saying this poem succeeds and that poem fails. I go back to the intention of the poet and the context in which the poem is presented. I work a lot in the schools with fourth graders and eighth graders and I’ve seen the work of poems happen. We write poems to change ourselves. The poem becomes a kind of residue, it marks a new insight.

The poems that seem to translate the experience of the poet to another listener use metaphors grounded in authentic truth. The language has specificity to it. The metaphor works at multiple levels. The figurative language accurately describes or points to, for instance, how root systems in the soil communicate and support one another toward the collective health of a forest. Ideally, this language has the vibrancy of a true conversation, which from Latin “conveyor” means “together to turn.” We forget when reading where your idea ends and my idea begins. We’re caught up in this decentralized collective effort to move an idea further or to hit upon phrasing for an expression.

Are there poems either from The Nature of Our Times or otherwise, that you feel meaningfully changed a conservation outcome? Or would you not measure it in that way?

There’s a great phrase that Jane Hirshfield used: She says perhaps poems are the lichens of activism. And one of the things about lichens is that the work they’re doing is often very, very, very slow, often subtle, and often unseen. I think the same can be true of poems. It’s not so easy to say, “Ah, two weeks later, you changed your behavior.” And there’s something about the arts and poetry that resists scientific inquiry.

So this is also pushing against a tension that I think is interesting. So many questions of the spirit are not answerable or provable. Donald Hall says, “Poems are the unsayable said.” What he’s pointing at is the tyranny of what we can measure. Rebecca Solnit talks about this. We can be tyrannized by only believing in what we can absolutely measure. And then suddenly, we’re feeling deprived of spiritual life, because that’s what we can’t measure.

I think poems flirt with that notion of “let’s be patient like lichen. Let’s be tolerant of things that don’t have an easy answer.” Maybe the work of lichens is that work of breaking rocks, slowly making soil. It’s the creative, productive work of decomposition. There’s an element of poems breaking our rigid ways of thinking and feeling and opening up new possibilities that we don’t quite fit into yet. We don’t know when that’s gonna change our behavior. We never quite are certain about it. But they’re pulling us in and they’re making us pause. And in that pause, we suddenly have room for new thought or for making a connection we would never have made before or for simply questioning a very rigid way of thinking that we always carried for so long.

Towards the end of the essay, you suggest that we need research into which kinds of artistic approaches and collaborations could have real impact. 

What I'm saying is take caution. Research with patience. This is not supposed to be easy. We don’t need to be overly ambitious. James Pennebaker’s research from 30 years ago about journaling and the power of using language to process grief, it moved the needle. It wasn’t overshooting in its statements. How do we find the appropriate way to engage in research that can bring other people into the conversation? We’re a small group, the world of poets. Talk about a bubble. Nobody inside it needs convincing. “Look at this poem. Oh, I love that poem. You know, that reminds me of this poem.” Nobody’s asking, “Where’s your data?”

If you were to fantasize about a first study in this vein, one that can sort out what kinds of collaborations between poets and scientists might change behavior, what would it look like?

I’ve spent 30 years going into the community. At the Wick Poetry Center, we like to say that we bring poetry to people’s everyday lives. We want people to encounter a poem who would never go to a bookstore and buy a small book of poems. They’d never think of themselves as writers or readers of poetry. We love to introduce it to them in a friendly way that invites them in.

During the pandemic, we worked with nurses and we brought poems about nursing for an incredible project we called “Sacred Breath,” and another project called “Some Days.” And we invited nurses to write their own reflections inspired by a model poem about their experiences. And we didn’t say it has to be a poem, but many of them ended up writing beautiful phrases and images in metaphors that is the work of poetry. They weren’t fearful that they could be judged. We pulled them into a conversation through poetry about their profession and their life experiences that were emotionally charged and needed an outlet. Why not do that with the environmental movement or with climate change? Could we set up a group where we’re studying how it affects people’s ways of thinking? When we change our thinking, we change our behavior.

What impact are you hoping the first Poetry for Science gathering in a few weeks will have?

We have this incredible group of featured speakers: Phillip Levin, Jane Lubchenco, the former head of NOAA, Melissa Nelson, who’s an Indigenous environment ecologist. And wonderful poets. We will be celebrating this collective work that so many of us have been doing. We were inspired to create this intentional space and time for people to come together because we were learning about this work happening in so many areas around our country and around the world. Our hope is that we create the time and the space for people to meet one another, to share ideas, to be inspired by each other, and then leave the gathering and have new relationships that can help us form new collaborations.

We’re creating an online community directory where people can, if they wish, post their project, their research interest and their contact information, either as poet, artist or scientist, and it can be searchable. We want to provide more momentum to this collective movement that has been building for 14 or 15 years in a decentralized way. Nobody’s ever called it out and named it until now. There is power in naming, and this Poets for Science gathering is halfway between an academic conference and a festival. It’s a gathering because we’re gathering the resources that we all carry within us and we want people to share their expertise, their knowledge, their passion with each other.

title: Romance Scam Prevention Act Signed into Law
content:
Last week, President Trump signed into law the Romance Scam Prevention Act that Congressman David Valadao (CA-22) introduced and that received bipartisan sponsorship. In short, this new federal law requires dating apps and services to notify users who have interacted with someone who was removed for fraudulent activity.

The scale of romance scams is enormous, with Americans losing $1.5 billion in 2025 as per the FTC and global losses coming in yearly at over $1 trillion. Dating apps play a significant role in the phenomenon because they present predators with the perfect pool in which to fish for victims. According to a year-long investigation whose results were released in recent weeks, U.S. Sen. Maggie Hassan concluded that Match Group has greatly lagged behind in its efforts to implement the best technological safeguards available. This is especially relevant because Match Group (which controls most of the best-known dating apps such as Tinder, Hinge, and OkCupid) continues to dominate the dating app market and hence its failures put many users at risk.

The new legislation may help users who are still in touch off-app with fraudsters who have been removed. That is a very narrow slice of users, however, and the system largely depends on whether dating apps effectively remove said fraudsters in the first place. The Romance Scam Prevention Act, however, places no obligations on apps to remove fraudsters or to prevent their joining apps in the first place. It is theoretically possible that the passage of even this fairly weak dating-app-related legislation, in conjunction with the issuance of Sen. Hassan's report, will put some pressure on apps and signal that stricter laws could follow if they don't improve their safety measures. As of now, however, the new law itself is unlikely to stop more than a minimal percentage of romance scams.

Last, it is worth mentioning that financial harm to dating app users, while very important, is far from the only damage resulting from dating apps' continued lackluster use of safeguards. For a crucial example, according to a Columbia Journalism Investigations survey, one third of women who use dating apps report having been sexually assaulted or raped by someone they met on an app. Neither the Romance Scam Prevention Act nor other congressional action so far addresses these many acts of violence or other related harms.

title: ICE is Now Even More Unpopular than the IRS
author: IlyaSomin
content:
A recent Pew Research Center survey finds that Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) is by far the most unpopular federal agency, easily outstripping even the widely despised IRS. According to Pew, 56% of Americans disapprove of ICE, compared to only 35% who approve. That's substantially worse than the IRS (which is disapproved by only a 46-37 margin).

Other recent surveys show growing public support for abolishing ICE. For example, a July YouGov poll indicates that 48% support abolition, compared to 40% who oppose it. Another survey,  conducted in March of this year, showed a similar 50-39 margin in favor of abolition.

The fact that ICE is unpopular doesn't by itself prove the agency should be abolished. Having written a book and many other publications on widespread public ignorance about government policy, I would be the last to argue that popularity is a good metric of a policy's - or an agency's - merit. But, in this case, public opinion is right. As I explained in an August 2025 article in The Hill, and a follow-up piece for the Boston Globe, (non-paywalled version here), ICE's many abuses do indeed justify abolishing it. And the case for doing so has been strengthened by more recent events, such as the brutal killing of two US citizens in Minnesota.

While ICE abuses have been exacerbated by the policies of the second Trump Administration, many predate it, and are inherent in the entire enterprise of mass deportation.

As explained in my article in The Hill, abolishing ICE would not completely end interior deportations. But it would make them heavily dependent on the cooperation of state and local governments, thereby strengthening constitutional federalism and reducing incentives for abuse, at least to a significant degree.

In that article, I also explain how support for abolition be further bolstered by combining it with shifting ICE funds to state and local law enforcement. This undermines the principal political obstacle to abolition: the fear that getting rid of ICE would increase crime. Transferring the funds to state and local police would help defuse such concerns, win the support of law enforcement agencies, and foster genuine reductions in violent and property crimes; social science evidence shows that putting more police on the streets has that effect, whereas deportations do not.

title: Visiting Slate’s first showroom as its $25,000 electric truck nears production
content:
I was hoping there would be at least two Slate Trucks on site so I could compare build quality between trucks and check things like panel gaps, window operation, and chassis creaks. But only one truck was on display. And it wasn’t close to a production model; rather, the black Slate Truck was a hand-built older prototype with a black wrap (the Slate Truck base color is gray). The bed and passenger sides were cordoned off, but the driver-side door was open so shoppers could hop in and check out the interior.

It was bigger than I expected—to my eye, roughly the size of a Hyundai Santa Cruz. The tailgate was down, and it felt reassuringly sturdy when I pressed down on it. The 5-foot-long (152.4 cm) bed floor looked and felt durable, not much different from any other pickup on the market.

I really wanted to jump up and down on the tailgate. But I couldn’t even sit on it. Eric Bangeman/Ars Technica

The exterior passed the eye test, with the panels appearing well-fitted. The doors sat flush with the surrounding body panels when closed. Of course, I was looking at a prototype carefully built to be poked and prodded by automotive reporters and the general public, so the level of fit and finish was no surprise. The challenge for Slate will be getting consistent build quality with minimal panel gaps, watertight seals, consistent door-to-fender transitions, and hood/frunk alignment. The Slate assembly line in Warsaw, Indiana, is still making prototyping runs at this point, Purdy told me, and the company is hoping to start on production models “soon.”

I hopped inside the cab once I got the opportunity, and the door closed with a solid-sounding “thunk.” It’s spartan inside, with a small screen for the instrument panel, a phone holder, physical climate controls, and window winders. The seats were both supportive and comfortable, and, after moving my seat, I had ample legroom. While the seat slid back and forth smoothly, the seatback recline lever on the side didn’t work.

The shopping experience

Beyond the default Blank Slate body style, Slate offers two SUV options—the Squareback SUV and Fastback SUV—and an open-air kit. I asked Purdy if they were selling any of the SUVs. “Most customers are going with the truck configuration,” he said. “And then they’re customizing their trucks in the Slate Garage.”
